doc.title: Bobby Johnson Jr. interviewed by Monk Rowe, Ellenville, New York, June 23, 1998

title: Jim Crow in the South and playing with white musicians
summary: He discusses which states were worst, surviving insults, and how playing downtown with white musicians became unremarkable.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Was there certain parts of the country that were worse than others as far as race? © Fillius Jazz Archive -7-

Well, when you way worse than the others, most people would say that Mississippi was the worst place in the world to be, on any planet. But not really, it was four or five states that had awful what we called Jim Crow laws. But a lot of people could survive. I have been insulted when I was a young fellow, but I survived because my mother used to tell me all the time she says just get along with people and everything will come all right, because naturally she never wanted anything to happen to me. I’ve seen some awful things happen to people in the south. But it was just a part of our country of growing up, you know what I mean? It was a part of our culture, of being what we are today. And maybe, I couldn’t say it was for the best, but I can say that everything’s going to be all right. It’s going to be better, you know? And one of the main things that I like to see was like I told, I was one of the first ones, like they used to say whatever happened to Bobby? And people would say oh man he’s downtown playing with the white boys. Well that was true. But nowadays, even a saying like that is passé. People don’t even say it like that. If you’re good enough to play with anyone, you can play, and like in colleges and different things like that, social circles. And nowadays if a musician is talented, he can play with anyone. And I like to see, I have had several seminars with college kids you know, and I have never actually felt anyone was any other different color than mine, other than playing. And that’s what I wanted to see. As you know, the University of Florida down in Gainesville, they had great bands down there, and the University of Florida A&M, that’s where the Adderley brothers came from. We introduced them. The Erskine Hawkins band — can I tell the story?
